pathophysiology.summary: Airway inflammation and oedema narrow the bronchial lumen. Bronchial smooth-muscle constriction causes variable expiratory airflow obstruction. Mucus plugging increases ventilation–perfusion mismatch. Progressive respiratory-muscle fatigue and rising carbon dioxide signal impending respiratory failure.
keyMechanisms: Airway inflammation and oedema cause mucosal swelling and luminal narrowing.
Bronchospasm restricts expiratory airflow and causes hyperinflation.
Mucus plugging and local atelectasis impair gas exchange.
Respiratory-muscle fatigue can lead to alveolar hypoventilation, hypercapnia and respiratory failure.

symptoms: Recurrent wheeze, persistent cough, dyspnoea, chest tightness and reduced feeding or activity.
physicalSigns: Tachypnoea, intercostal or subcostal retractions, accessory-muscle use, polyphonic wheeze, reduced air entry and low baseline oxygen saturation.
redFlags: Unable to speak a few words, central cyanosis, exhaustion, altered consciousness, silent chest, severe bradycardia or poor response to initial Short-Acting Beta-2 Agonist (SABA) therapy.
precipitants: Viral upper respiratory tract infection, environmental allergens, tobacco smoke or vaping exposure, airborne pollutants, poor controller adherence and incorrect inhaler or spacer technique.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Acute airway, breathing or circulatory compromise with urticaria, angioedema or gastrointestinal distress; give immediate Intramuscular (IM) adrenaline (epinephrine) and manage the airway and circulation.
Sudden unwitnessed choking, stridor or focal/unilateral findings such as monophonic wheeze or asymmetric air entry; seek urgent paediatric bronchoscopy assessment.

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Oxygen saturation, retractions, scalene use, air entry and wheeze
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Record at baseline and after treatment to guide disposition.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced saturation, especially below 92% in severe distress
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Give oxygen when hypoxaemic and maintain the locally specified target during transfer.

ruleIn.testName: Serial respiratory rate and work of breathing
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Persistent tachypnoea, severe recession, accessory-muscle use or decreasing effort
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Repeat with PRAM after bronchodilator therapy and escalate deterioration.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Markedly reduced flow with bronchodilator reversibility
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Use only in a cooperative child, typically aged 5 years or older, without delaying emergency treatment.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Carbon-dioxide retention, hypercapnia, acidaemia or severe refractory hypoxaemia
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Reserve for life-threatening features, exhaustion, altered sensorium or failure to respond to maximal therapy.

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Identified pathogen when the result changes isolation or treatment
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Do not use routinely; antibiotics are not indicated for an uncomplicated asthma attack.

ruleOut.targetCondition: Pneumothorax, lobar collapse, foreign body or focal consolidation
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Focal consolidation, pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum when an alternative or complication is suspected
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Routine radiography is not recommended for a typical responding attack.

clinicalManagement.title: ABCDE survey with concurrent correction
actions: Work through Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability and Exposure in order, and correct each abnormality concurrently as it is found: do not wait for the full survey, investigations or a diagnosis before treating a life-threatening problem, and call for senior help early.

Airway: look, listen and feel for obstruction; open it with a neutral head position (head tilt in older children) or jaw thrust, suction secretions, use an oropharyngeal airway if unconscious and call for expert paediatric airway help if it cannot be kept patent.

Breathing: count respiratory rate, measure SpO2, check recession, grunting, nasal flaring and air entry; if SpO2 is below 94% give [💊 Oxygen | 10–15 L/min via reservoir mask | Inhaled | Continuous | Until SpO2 94–98%, then titrate to target] and treat life-threatening chest problems as they are found.

Circulation: check heart rate, capillary refill and blood pressure, attach a monitor and secure IV access if the attack is severe (PRAM 8–12); if shocked give [💊 Sodium chloride 0.9% | 10 mL/kg | IV or IO bolus over 10 minutes | Reassess after each bolus; repeat if still shocked | Until perfusion restored].

Disability: assess responsiveness (alert, voice, pain, unresponsive), pupils and posture, and measure capillary glucose; if glucose is below 3 mmol/L give [💊 Glucose 10% | 2 mL/kg | IV or IO bolus | Repeat after 10 minutes if glucose remains below 3 mmol/L | Until glucose 3 mmol/L or above]; look for seizure activity.
Exposure: expose the child to examine fully while preventing heat loss; check temperature, skin (rash, bruising, wounds) and abdomen, then cover again.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess severity and start bronchodilation
actions: Calculate and record the initial PRAM score and oxygen saturation.
Screen for Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission history or near-fatal asthma risk factors.
Give [💊 Oxygen | 10–15 L/min via reservoir mask | Inhaled | Continuous | Until SpO2 94–98%, then titrate to target] if hypoxaemic.

Start inhaled short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) treatment: [💊 Salbutamol | 4–8 puffs by MDI with spacer, or weight/severity-based nebulisation | Inhaled | Every 20 minutes for the first hour, then titrate to response | First hour and reassessment thereafter].

clinicalManagement.title: First-hour treatment
actions: Repeat [💊 Salbutamol | 4–8 puffs by MDI with spacer (oxygen-driven nebulisation for severe attacks) | Inhaled | Every 20 minutes for three doses | First hour].

For moderate or severe exacerbations add [💊 Ipratropium bromide | 4 puffs by MDI with spacer or 250 micrograms by nebuliser | Inhaled | Every 20 minutes during the first hour, maximum three doses | First hour only].

For moderate-to-severe attacks or a poor initial response to SABA give early [💊 Prednisolone | 1–2 mg/kg (maximum 20 mg under 2 years, 30 mg at 2–5 years, 60 mg at 5–12 years) | PO | Once daily | 3–5 days total].

clinicalManagement.title: Reassess and decide disposition
actions: Repeat PRAM and reassess oxygen saturation and work of breathing.

For PRAM 8–12 or worsening, escalate immediately to the paediatric critical-care or ICU team and consider [💊 Magnesium sulfate | 40 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) | IV infusion over 20 minutes | Single dose in the ED | Single dose] under continuous cardiac monitoring.

For PRAM 1–3 with sustained response, use the discharge pathway: [💊 Salbutamol | 2–4 puffs by MDI with spacer | Inhaled | Every 4–6 hours for 24 hours, then as needed | 24 hours, then as needed], the inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) plan, spacer demonstration, written asthma action plan and review within 7 days.

regimens.dose: 4–8 puffs by MDI with spacer, or weight/severity-based nebulisation
regimens.frequency: Every 20 minutes for the first hour, then titrate to response
adjustments: Use oxygen-driven nebulisation if MDI with spacer is not feasible.
monitoring: PRAM, heart rate and oxygen saturation.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity; use caution with severe tachyarrhythmia.

regimens.indication: Moderate or severe attack during the first hour
regimens.patientGroup: Children with PRAM-directed moderate or severe attack
regimens.dose: 4 puffs by MDI with spacer or 250 micrograms by nebuliser
regimens.frequency: Every 20 minutes for the first hour; maximum three doses
adjustments: Use local device equivalence and infection-control policy.
monitoring: PRAM, heart rate and dry mouth.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ipratropium or atropine derivatives.

regimens.indication: Moderate or severe attack or poor initial SABA response
regimens.dose: 1–2 mg/kg; maximum 20 mg under 2 years, 30 mg at 2–5 years and 60 mg at 5–12 years
adjustments: Seek specialist advice if oral treatment is not tolerated.
monitoring: Clinical response, vomiting and glucose in high-risk children.
contraindications: Hypersensitivity; evaluate active serious infection while treating the emergency.

regimens.indication: Refractory severe attack with PRAM 8–12 after initial treatment
adjustments: Use only under paediatric critical-care or local emergency protocol.
monitoring: Continuous cardiac monitoring, blood pressure, deep tendon reflexes and weakness.
contraindications: Severe renal failure, atrioventricular block or neuromuscular disease.

guidedApproach.title: Pediatric Respiratory Assessment Measure (PRAM): purpose and use
guidedApproach.prompt: PRAM is a validated, standardized clinical scoring tool used in the Emergency Department (ED) and acute-care settings for children aged 2–17 years.
guidedApproach.guidance:
Unlike Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) or spirometry, PRAM uses objective physical-examination findings and pulse oximetry and does not require a cooperative child.
The score ranges from 0 to 12 and evaluates suprasternal retractions, scalene muscle contraction, air entry, wheezing and oxygen saturation. Suprasternal retractions and scalene contraction are binary: 0 absent or 2 present.
Scoring reference: suprasternal retractions absent 0/present 2; scalene contraction absent 0/present 2; air entry normal 0, decreased at bases 1, decreased at apex and base 2, minimal or absent/silent chest 3; wheezing absent 0, expiratory only 1, inspiratory and expiratory 2, audible without a stethoscope or silent chest 3; oxygen saturation is scored against the applicable room-air thresholds in the validated PRAM reference and local pathway.

guidedApproach.title: PRAM severity classification and clinical interpretation
guidedApproach.prompt: Use the total PRAM score to guide immediate treatment and escalation while retaining clinical judgement.
guidedApproach.guidance:
Mild exacerbation (PRAM 1–3): minimal work of breathing, near-normal air entry and oxygen saturation at or above the local target; continue SABA, assess response and consider discharge only when all discharge criteria are met.
Moderate exacerbation (PRAM 4–7): moderate accessory-muscle use, localized reduction in air entry and oxygen saturation in the locally defined moderate range; repeat SABA, add ipratropium bromide and give early oral systemic corticosteroid when indicated.
Severe exacerbation or impending failure (PRAM 8–12): severe retractions, widespread reduction in air entry or silent chest and severe hypoxaemia; provide oxygen-driven bronchodilator treatment, adjunctive ipratropium and corticosteroid therapy according to protocol, monitor continuously and obtain immediate paediatric critical-care or Intensive Care Unit (ICU) advice.
The pasted severity thresholds and treatment associations remain pending clinician verification.

guidedApproach.title: PRAM timing and utility in the ED pathway
guidedApproach.prompt: Repeat PRAM at defined points to document response and support disposition.
guidedApproach.guidance:
Baseline assessment (triage/time 0): establish initial severity and treatment intensity.
Post-treatment reassessment (60 minutes): reassess after the first hour of bronchodilator therapy.
Disposition: PRAM 1–3 with sustained response may support discharge when oxygenation, work of breathing, caregiver education and follow-up criteria are satisfied; PRAM 4–7 with partial response requires continued ED observation/treatment or paediatric admission; PRAM 8–12 or a worsening score requires escalation to paediatric critical care or ICU.

pitfalls: Relying on routine chest radiographs or blood gas testing in a responding attack.
Discharging without confirming spacer technique and issuing a written asthma action plan.
keyPoints: Treat first, then reassess at 1 hour.
A silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion or altered consciousness is life-threatening.

patientEducation: Demonstrate correct MDI and spacer technique.
Provide a written asthma action plan with daily ICS controller and rescue SABA instructions.
Counsel on avoiding tobacco smoke, vaping and known triggers.
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid environmental tobacco smoke, vaping and known triggers.
mdtReferrals: Paediatric Emergency Department, respiratory team and critical care for severe or poorly responding attacks.
dischargeCriteria: PRAM 1–3 sustained for at least 1–2 hours, oxygen saturation above 94% on room air, stable work of breathing and caregiver able to execute the home plan.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Arrange primary-care or specialist paediatric asthma-clinic review within 7 days.
